desc:
An exchange desk deals in n currencies numbered 0 to n - 1. Each rates[i] = [from, to, num, den] says that one unit of currency from can be converted into exactly num / den units of currency to. Only the listed directions are available, a conversion can be used any number of times, and amounts may be fractional.

An arbitrage is a closed loop of conversions that starts and ends in the same currency and leaves you with strictly more of it than you started with. Return true if an arbitrage exists and false otherwise. A loop that returns exactly what you started with is not an arbitrage.

Example: n = 3, rates = [[0,1,2,1],[1,2,3,1],[2,0,1,5]]. One unit of 0 becomes 2 units of 1, then 6 units of 2, then 6/5 units of 0, which is more than 1, so the answer is true. With the last rate 1/7 the loop returns 6/7, so the answer is false.
constraints: rates[i] = [from, to, num, den] with 0 ≤ from, to < n, from ≠ to and 1 ≤ num, den ≤ 1,000
Each ordered pair (from, to) appears at most once
hints: A loop gains money exactly when the product of its rates is greater than 1. Products are awkward; how can multiplication become addition?

Taking logarithms turns 'product > 1' into 'sum of log-rates > 0', that is, a positive cycle. Negating gives a negative cycle, which Bellman-Ford can detect. Floating point can misjudge loops whose product is exactly 1, though.

Stay exact: keep for each currency the best product so far as a fraction (numerator, denominator), start every currency at 1/1, and relax with best[u] * rate > best[v] using integer cross-multiplication. In each round read the values of the previous round. If an improvement is still possible in round n, there is a profitable loop.
editorial: Model currencies as nodes and conversions as directed edges. A closed loop is profitable when the product of its rates exceeds 1. Instead of minimising a sum of weights, Bellman-Ford can maximise a product: start every currency with value 1 (as if a free virtual source led to each currency), and repeatedly relax value[v] = max(value[v], value[u] * rate), computing each round from the values of the previous round. After round j, value[v] is the best product over chains of at most j conversions. Without a profitable loop the values settle after n - 1 rounds, because an optimal chain never repeats a currency (cutting out a loop of product at most 1 cannot hurt). If round n still improves something, a chain of n conversions beats every shorter chain, and since it repeats a currency it contains a profitable loop.

Floating-point logarithms are the textbook shortcut, but a loop whose product is exactly 1 (for example 2/1 followed by 1/2, or long telescoping chains) may come out as 1.0000000000000002 and be wrongly reported. With integer rates you can avoid the problem completely by storing each value as an unreduced pair (a, b) and comparing a1 * b2 > a2 * b1; Python integers do not overflow, and because every round uses only the previous round's values, numbers have at most about 10 bits per conversion in the chain, so they stay small. With at most 50 currencies and 600 rates the work is about 50 · 600 big-integer multiplications. Time O(n · E) operations, space O(n).
solution:
def hasArbitrage(n, rates):
    num = [1] * n
    den = [1] * n
    for _ in range(n):
        nn = num[:]
        dd = den[:]
        changed = False
        for u, v, a, b in rates:
            x = num[u] * a
            y = den[u] * b
            if x * dd[v] > nn[v] * y:
                nn[v], dd[v] = x, y
                changed = True
        if not changed:
            return False
        num, den = nn, dd
    return True
